title: Equity securities: ownership, preferred, and the vocabulary the exam assumes

reading.body:
Owning stock means owning a slice of a company. The exam uses four different share counts. Mix them up and you lose points.

**Authorized** is the most shares the corporate charter allows. To raise it, shareholders must vote. **Issued** is how many of those shares the company has sold. **Treasury** is issued shares the company bought back and now holds. **Outstanding** is the number in public hands right now. Outstanding shares vote, collect dividends, and count in earnings per share.

Keep one formula: **Outstanding = Issued − Treasury.**

Worked example. A charter authorizes 1,000,000 shares. The company issues 500,000 shares. It then buys back 100,000 shares. Now 500,000 shares are still **issued**, 100,000 shares sit in **treasury**, and **400,000 shares are outstanding**. The other 500,000 shares were never sold. They are authorized but unissued.

reading.h: Treasury stock is issued but not outstanding
reading.body:
Treasury stock is the classic trap. When a company buys back shares, those shares **do not vote, get no dividend, and drop out of the EPS count**. But they are still counted as **issued**. The exam offers the wrong answer "treasury stock is no longer issued." It is issued. It is just not outstanding.

Why buy back stock? Fewer shares outstanding split the same earnings among fewer shares, so **EPS rises**. Say a company earns $10 million on 5 million shares. EPS is $2.00. Buy back to 4 million shares and EPS is $2.50. The actual earnings did not change.

A share has three separate values. The exam checks that you do not confuse them.

**Par (or stated) value** is an accounting figure, often $0.01 or $1 per share. It has no link to market price. Common stock can even be no-par.

**Book value** is the net worth behind each share. Take equity, subtract preferred and intangibles, then divide by common shares. It is what a share would claim in liquidation at balance-sheet values.

**Market value** is what the stock trades at. Supply and demand set it. Par has no link to book. Book has no link to market. Learn that, and a whole set of "which is TRUE" questions falls apart.

reading.h: What a common stockholder actually gets
reading.body:
Common stockholders own the company. They hold a set of rights.

They **vote** for directors and on major matters: mergers, stock splits, more authorized shares, and new convertibles or warrants. They get a **pro-rata share of dividends**, but only if and when the board declares them. Dividends are never guaranteed. They have the right to **inspect the books**. They have the **preemptive right** to buy new shares first and keep their percentage. They have a **residual claim** in liquidation. They are paid last, after every creditor and every preferred holder.

The exam tests two limits. Stockholders do **not** vote on whether a dividend is paid. The board decides that. Stockholders also do **not** hire officers. Because of **limited liability**, a shareholder can lose only what they put in, never the company's debts. Pay $2,000 for shares that fall to zero, and your maximum loss is $2,000.

reading.h: Preferred stock: equity that behaves like a bond
reading.body:
Preferred stock is still ownership, but it acts like a bond. It pays a **fixed dividend**, stated as a percent of par (usually $100 par) or as a dollar amount. It has priority over common for both dividends and liquidation. It **usually has no vote**. A 6% $100-par preferred pays $6 per year.

The payment is fixed and there is no maturity date. So preferred prices move opposite to interest rates, like a long bond. **Current yield = annual dividend ÷ market price.** A $6 dividend on an $80 price is a 7.5% yield.

The main type here is **cumulative** preferred. Any skipped dividend piles up as **dividends in arrears**. The company must pay all of it before common gets a penny. **Straight (non-cumulative)** preferred loses a skipped dividend for good. Other types (participating, convertible, callable, adjustable-rate) get their full treatment in the Series 7 depth module.

Both let you buy the issuer's stock at a set price. But they are opposites.

**Rights** come from the company's own **preemptive right**. Existing shareholders get one right per share. The subscription price sits **below** market, so the right has value right away. Rights are **short-lived**, about 30 to 90 days.

**Warrants** are long-term "sweeteners." A company attaches them to a bond or preferred offering to make it sell. The exercise price sits **above** market at issue. So at first a warrant has **only time value and no intrinsic value**. Warrants can last for years, and some never expire.

Neither one pays dividends or votes. Memory hook: rights are short, below market, with value now. Warrants are long, above market, a bet on later.

reading.h: ADRs, dividends, and why splits create nothing
reading.body:
An **ADR** (American Depositary Receipt) is a receipt from a U.S. bank for a set number of foreign shares it holds abroad. It lets Americans buy foreign stock **in U.S. dollars**, on U.S. markets, with dividends paid in dollars. The catch the exam tests: **currency risk remains**. A weaker foreign currency lowers the dollar value of both the dividend and the ADR. ADR holders usually **do not vote**.

Dividends follow four dates: **D**eclaration, **E**x-dividend, **R**ecord, **P**ayable. Buy on or after the ex-date and you do **not** get the dividend.

A **stock split** just re-cuts the pie. 100 shares at $80 in a 2-for-1 split become 200 shares at $40, still $8,000. Total value and total cost basis do **not** change. A split creates no wealth. Restricted stock sold under **Rule 144** needs a **6-month** holding period for a reporting company. Lock that number in now.

flashcards.back: Outstanding = Issued − Treasury. Outstanding shares are the ones that vote, get dividends, and count in EPS.
No vote, no dividend, left out of EPS. Still counted as ISSUED, just not outstanding.

flashcards.front: Par vs. book vs. market value
flashcards.back: Par = an accounting number. Book = net worth per share. Market = trading price. The three have no link.

flashcards.front: Do common stockholders vote on dividends?
flashcards.back: No. The board declares dividends. Shareholders vote on directors, mergers, splits, more authorized shares, and new convertibles or warrants.
A stockholder can lose only what they put in. They are never liable for the company's debts.
Secured creditors → unsecured creditors → subordinated debt → preferred stock → common stock (residual, last).
Cumulative: skipped dividends pile up as arrears and must be paid before common. Straight: a skipped dividend is gone for good.
Current yield = annual dividend ÷ market price. Price and yield move opposite ways, like a long bond.
Rights: to existing holders, below market, short-lived (30 to 90 days), value now. Warrants: sweetener, above market at issue, long-term, only time value.

flashcards.front: ADR — one thing that is TRUE
flashcards.back: Trades and pays dividends in U.S. dollars. The holder STILL has currency risk and usually cannot vote.

flashcards.front: Does a stock split change total value?
flashcards.back: No. More shares at a lower price. Total value and total cost basis do not change.
6 months for restricted stock of an SEC-reporting company (1 year if non-reporting).

quiz.stem: A corporation repurchases some of its previously issued shares and holds them as treasury stock. These treasury shares:
options: Continue to vote and receive dividends until they are cancelled
Are no longer counted as issued shares
Carry no voting rights and receive no dividends
Increase the number of shares outstanding
quiz.explanation: Treasury stock is issued but not outstanding: no vote, no dividend, excluded from EPS. The trap is 'no longer issued' — it remains issued (outstanding = issued − treasury), and a buyback reduces outstanding shares, it does not increase them.

quiz.stem: You paid $2,000 for shares of a company. The company later goes bankrupt and its stock becomes worthless. What is the most you can lose?
options: The $2,000 plus your share of the company's unpaid debts
The $2,000 you paid for the shares
Nothing, because the company must refund shareholders before paying creditors
The $2,000 plus any dividends you received in the past
quiz.explanation: Limited liability caps a stockholder's loss at the amount invested — $2,000 — and never extends to corporate debts. Creditors are paid before shareholders in liquidation, so there is no refund; past dividends are already yours to keep.

quiz.stem: A company has both preferred and common stock. Compared with a common stockholder, a preferred stockholder generally:
options: Has more votes at shareholder meetings
Shares fully in all of the company's future growth in profits
Receives a fixed dividend before common stockholders receive anything
Can require the company to buy the shares back at any time
quiz.explanation: Preferred pays a fixed dividend with priority over common for dividends and in liquidation. It usually has no vote (so 'more votes' is wrong) and does not share in earnings growth (that is common's upside); only callable preferred can be redeemed, and that is the issuer's option, not the holder's.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is TRUE of warrants but NOT of stock rights?
options: The exercise price is typically set above the stock's market price when issued
Holders receive dividends on the underlying stock
They are issued to existing shareholders so they can maintain proportionate ownership
They typically expire within 30 to 90 days
quiz.explanation: Warrants are long-term sweeteners with an exercise price ABOVE market at issue (only time value). Rights go to existing holders below market and expire in 30–90 days, so options C and D describe rights. Neither warrants nor rights pay dividends, so B is false for both.

quiz.stem: An investor buys an ADR representing shares of a Japanese company. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Dividends are paid to the investor in Japanese yen
The investor has no exposure to changes in the yen-dollar exchange rate
The ADR can be traded only on the Tokyo exchange
Dividends are paid in U.S. dollars, but the investor still bears currency risk
quiz.explanation: ADRs trade and pay dividends in U.S. dollars on U.S. markets, but because the underlying shares and dividends are denominated in yen, a weaker yen lowers the dollar value of both — currency risk remains. That kills options A, B, and C.

quiz.stem: You own 100 shares of a stock trading at $80. The company announces a 2-for-1 stock split. Immediately after the split, you have:
options: 200 shares worth about $40 each, about $8,000 in total
200 shares worth $80 each, about $16,000 in total
100 shares worth $160 each, about $16,000 in total
50 shares worth $160 each, about $8,000 in total
quiz.explanation: A 2-for-1 forward split doubles the shares and halves the price: 200 shares at $40 = $8,000, unchanged from the original 100 × $80. A split creates no value, so the $16,000 answers are traps; fewer shares at a higher price would be a reverse split.

quiz.stem: A customer wants stocks whose earnings tend to hold up even during a recession. Which category BEST fits?
options: Cyclical stocks such as automakers and steel producers
Speculative stocks such as early-stage biotech companies
Growth stocks that reinvest all of their earnings
Defensive stocks such as food producers and utilities
quiz.explanation: Defensive (non-cyclical) stocks sell goods with stable demand regardless of the economy — food, utilities, pharma. Cyclical stocks are the opposite (they track the business cycle), and growth and speculative names carry more risk, not stability.
